To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the effect, “similar-to-me,” occurs in simulated employment interviews; (2) the effect is more likely to occur in the evaluations of applicants who have biographical information in common with the evaluators; (3) the effect is less likely to occur when evaluators are prejudiced; and (4) the effect is not likely to occur when applicants and evaluators are of the same race.

(a) biographical similarity between interviewer and applicant leads to higher ratings of a candidate's job suitability, and (b) racial prejudice is a major factor in determining the ratings of all candidates regardless or the applicant's race.

(a) the effect “similar to me” is not a general phenomenon that applies in all circumstances; (b) the effect is not a function of the applicant's racial background; (c) it is a function of the interviewer's background, particularly his or her need for affiliation and level of racial prejudice; (d) the effect is a function of both interviewer and applicant characteristics; and (e) the effect is stronger in the employment interview situation than in the classroom situation.

the effect of similarity between interviewer and applicant on the interviewer's evaluation of the applicant.
the effect of biographical similarity of the interviewer and the applicant on interview evaluations of job suitability and personal characteristics.
the effect, “similar-to-me,” in employment interviews.
